name: Premature Atrial Contractions
preview_text: The flutter of a stressed-out liver, the heavy thud of damp phlegm, and the weak skip of depleted blood are three different PACs - and each responds to its own TCM treatment, often...
conventional_description: In Western medicine, premature atrial contractions are extra heartbeats that start in the heart's upper chambers (atria) and disrupt the normal rhythm. They are common and often harmless, but can feel like a fluttering, pounding, or skipped beat in the chest. PACs are usually diagnosed with an electrocardiogram (ECG) or a Holter monitor, and may be triggered by stress, caffeine, alcohol, or underlying heart conditions.
conventional_treatments: For most people with infrequent PACs and no underlying heart disease, no treatment is needed beyond lifestyle changes - reducing stimulants and managing stress. When PACs are frequent or bothersome, doctors may prescribe beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers to suppress the extra beats. In rare cases, a catheter ablation procedure may be considered if medications fail.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the heart's rhythm is governed by the Heart organ system, which houses the Shen (spirit). For a steady beat, the Heart needs abundant Qi and Blood. When these are depleted - by overwork, poor diet, or chronic worry - the heart may skip or flutter, especially with exertion. This is the classic Qi and Blood Deficiency pattern, where the heart simply lacks the fuel to beat smoothly.
But the heart doesn't work alone. The Spleen produces Qi and Blood from food; if digestion is weak, the heart starves. The Liver smooths the flow of Qi; stress and frustration can cause Qi to stagnate and press upward, disrupting the rhythm. The Kidneys store Yin and Yang; when Yin is low, empty heat rises to disturb the heart, and when Yang is weak, the heart lacks the fire to pump strongly.
Each of these organ imbalances creates a different quality of palpitation - a flutter with heat, a thud with cold, a tight sensation with stress.
Excess patterns also play a role. Phlegm from poor digestion can cloud the chest and obstruct the heart's channels, causing a heavy, stuck sensation with the skipped beats. Blood stasis - often from long-standing stagnation or injury - can physically block the vessels, leading to sharp pain and irregular rhythm. These are not just physical blockages; they also disturb the Heart Shen, making you feel restless and uneasy.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening carefully to the quality of the skipped beats and the sensations that come with them. They will ask whether the feeling is more of a flutter, a thud, or a racing pulse, and what makes it better or worse. This first conversation often points toward one of several distinct patterns, each with its own story.
If the palpitations are accompanied by deep tiredness, poor appetite, and a washed-out complexion, the practitioner suspects Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is often pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels weak or fine. This pattern reflects a simple lack of the nourishment the Heart needs to beat steadily.
When the person also feels restless, has a dry mouth at night, or notices warm palms and soles, the picture shifts to Empty-Heat from Yin Deficiency. Here the tongue body is red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. The Yin is too weak to anchor the Heart’s spirit, so an unsettling heat rises and disturbs the rhythm.
A heavy sensation in the chest, a feeling of mucus in the throat, and a foggy head point toward Damp-Phlegm blocking the chest. The tongue coating looks greasy and thick, and the pulse is slippery or irregular. The practitioner sees a pattern of turbid fluids gumming up the channels that should carry clear signals to the Heart.
If the skipped beats come with a sharp, fixed pain in the chest or a bruised sensation, the practitioner looks for Heart Blood Stagnation. The tongue may be dusky or show purple spots, and the pulse feels rough or hesitant. Stagnant blood physically obstructs the vessels, forcing the Heart to stumble over the blockage.
When palpitations flare with stress, irritability, and a tight or distended feeling along the ribcage, the focus turns to Liver Qi Stagnation. The tongue is often normal or slightly red on the edges, and the pulse is wiry. Emotional pressure knots the flow of Qi, and that tension transmits directly to the Heart.
Finally, a person who always feels cold, has chilly hands and feet, and notices that the skipped beats are worse when they are tired or chilled may have Heart Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep, slow, or irregular. The warming, driving force of the Heart has dimmed, so the beat becomes weak and unsteady.

patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep and going to bed early, Warm, nourishing meals, Gentle exercise (walking, tai chi, yoga), Stress reduction and emotional calm
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Heart needs a steady supply of Qi to beat with a strong, regular rhythm and enough Blood to anchor the mind. When Qi and Blood both run low-often from overwork, poor diet, or chronic worry-the Heart lacks the fuel it needs. The result is a fluttering or skipped-beat sensation, especially when you are tired or after even light activity, because your body's reserves are simply too depleted to keep the rhythm smooth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale body, may be slightly thin or show teeth marks on the edges; thin white coating. Pulse: Fine (thin) and weak, especially at the right Guan position (Spleen).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are produced from the food you eat and the rest you get. Overwork and irregular eating drain your reserves, while worry directly injures the Spleen-the organ responsible for turning food into Qi and Blood. Cold foods further weaken the Spleen's digestive fire. Rest, warm meals, and gentle movement, on the other hand, conserve and slowly rebuild your Qi and Blood. As these reserves fill, the Heart receives the steady nourishment it needs to beat calmly and regularly.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Build your meals around warm, cooked, easily digestible foods-think congees, soups, and stews with small amounts of high-quality protein. Include blood-nourishing ingredients like red dates, goji berries, dark leafy greens, black sesame, and a little grass-fed red meat or bone broth if your digestion allows. Avoid raw, cold foods and iced drinks, which weaken the Spleen's ability to generate Qi and Blood. Prioritize deep rest and a consistent sleep schedule; even a short afternoon nap can make a difference. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps Qi flow without depleting you. Protect yourself from mental overstrain by taking regular breaks and practising simple breathing exercises.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the body’s cooling, nourishing Yin fluids run low, they can no longer anchor the heart’s rhythm. The resulting emptiness allows a restless, low-grade heat to rise and disturb the Heart-Shen, triggering premature beats that often feel like a quick flutter with a wave of heat. This is why the palpitations tend to be worse in the evening or at night, when Yin should be most settled, and why they come with a dry mouth, a thin rapid pulse, and an unsettled feeling.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with cracks, little or no coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin deficiency means the body’s coolant is low, so anything that adds heat - spicy meals, alcohol, emotional fire, or burning the candle at both ends - fans the empty flame that agitates the heart. Cooling, moistening foods and early nights rebuild that coolant, while gentle movement and calm routines keep the flame low and steady.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Cool and moisten your body from the inside. Eat pears, lily bulb, millet, tofu, and black sesame; sip warm water or chrysanthemum tea throughout the day. Avoid spicy, fried, or barbecued foods, and cut back on coffee and alcohol. Go to bed by 10:30 pm - the hours before midnight are when Yin rebuilds itself. Gentle, flowing movement like tai chi or restorative yoga supports Yin without overheating the body.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen’s digestive power is weakened, fluids are not properly transported and instead accumulate as dampness. Over time, this dampness congeals into a sticky, turbid substance called phlegm. This phlegm can settle in the chest, physically obstructing the free flow of Heart Qi and Blood, which disrupts the heart’s natural rhythm and triggers the sensation of skipped or extra beats.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, thick white greasy coat, wet surface. Pulse: slippery (Hua), possibly soggy (Ru) in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm forms when the Spleen’s digestive function is overwhelmed by heavy, greasy, or cold foods, and by a sedentary lifestyle that fails to move Qi. These triggers create the very phlegm and dampness that obstruct the chest and disrupt the Heart. Light, warm meals and gentle exercise support the Spleen and help clear phlegm, while a dry environment prevents external dampness from adding to the internal burden.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid heavy, greasy, and cold foods that generate dampness. Focus on warm, cooked meals with mild spices like ginger and cardamom. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps move Qi and reduce phlegm accumulation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Blood flow becomes sluggish or stuck in the vessels that nourish the Heart, the Heart muscle itself is starved of smooth, nourishing circulation. This stagnation creates a physical blockage that disrupts the Heart's natural rhythm, causing it to beat prematurely or irregularly. The stabbing, fixed pain that often accompanies these skipped beats is a hallmark of Blood stasis pressing on the channels.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark or purple body with stasis spots; sublingual veins distended and dark blue-purple; thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 se) or knotted (结 jie), especially at the left Cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis is literally a slowing and congealing of Blood flow. Cold and inactivity cause further congealing, while warmth and movement thin and mobilize the Blood. Emotional stress tightens the chest and causes Qi stagnation; since Qi moves Blood, stagnant Qi leads directly to more Blood stasis. Releasing that stress and keeping the chest warm and mobile directly counteracts the root mechanism of this pattern.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Choose warm, cooked foods that gently move Blood, such as turmeric, ginger, black fungus, and dark leafy greens. Avoid cold and raw foods that can congeal Blood and worsen stasis. Gentle, regular exercise like walking or tai chi is essential to keep circulation moving, but avoid overexertion. Manage emotional stress through deep breathing or meditation, as frustration and worry can tighten the chest and slow Blood flow.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for keeping Qi flowing smoothly throughout the body. When stress, frustration, or suppressed emotions build up, the Liver Qi gets stuck and can no longer move freely. This stagnant energy often presses upward and disturbs the Heart, making the heartbeat feel irregular or fluttering - especially during moments of emotional tension. You may notice the skipped beats come on when you feel wound up, and fade when you relax.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body, red or purplish sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, most prominent at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the main driver of Liver Qi Stagnation - it causes the Qi to knot up and surge toward the Heart, triggering the palpitations. Calming activities and moderate movement gently unblock that stuck energy, allowing the Heart rhythm to settle. Stimulants like caffeine and alcohol add heat and further agitate the Qi, while regular, peaceful meals and routines support the Liver’s natural flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Make stress relief a daily practice - gentle walks, deep breathing, or journaling can all help keep Qi moving. Limit coffee, alcohol, and spicy foods, which can add heat and agitate the Heart. Eat plenty of leafy greens and lightly cooked vegetables, and try to eat at regular times without rushing.

patterns.why_this_happens: Heart Yang is the fire that warms your body and drives the heartbeat. When that fire dims, the Heart lacks the strength to pump blood smoothly, so it stumbles into extra beats. The same deficiency leaves your chest feeling stuffy and your hands and feet cold because warmth cannot reach them.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, especially at the left Cun (Heart) position; may be knotted (slow with irregular pauses).

Rest and warmth conserve Yang, while warm foods gently stoke the body's inner fire. Gentle movement encourages Qi to move without spending it, and calming the mind prevents fear from further chilling the Heart.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep your chest, back, and feet warm, especially in cold weather. Favor warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, ginger, cinnamon, lamb, and walnuts, and avoid cold, raw, and icy items. Gentle daily movement such as walking or Tai Chi helps Qi flow without depleting your reserves, but stop before you feel tired.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture stop my heart palpitations?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help reduce the frequency and intensity of PACs. It works by calming the nervous system, smoothing the flow of Qi, and addressing the specific pattern causing your palpitations. Many people feel a difference after just a few sessions, but consistent treatment over several weeks yields the most lasting results.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my heart medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but coordination with your doctor is essential. Some herbs, like Dan Shen, can have mild blood-thinning effects, so if you are on anticoagulants, both your TCM practitioner and cardiologist must be informed. Never stop or adjust your prescription medication without your doctor's guidance. Always bring a full list of your medications to your TCM consultation.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: For PACs, a typical course starts with weekly sessions for 6-8 weeks. After that, your practitioner will reassess and may space treatments further apart as your rhythm stabilizes. Deficiency patterns often need longer-term care, while excess patterns may resolve more quickly.

faqs.question: What does it mean if my palpitations are worse at night?
faqs.answer: Nighttime worsening often points to Yin Deficiency with Empty Heat. When the body's cooling, nourishing Yin is low, the relative heat rises and disturbs the Heart Shen, making you more aware of skipped beats when you lie down. This pattern is also associated with dry mouth, night sweats, and a red tongue with little coating.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my PACs are caused by anxiety?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, anxiety is often a sign of Liver Qi Stagnation or Heart Shen disturbance, both of which can directly trigger palpitations. Acupuncture and herbs that soothe the Liver and calm the Shen - such as Chai Hu Shu Gan San - can address both the emotional trigger and the physical symptom together.

faqs.question: Are there any foods I should avoid with PACs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Avoid or greatly reduce caffeine, alcohol, and spicy, greasy foods, as these can stir up internal heat or create phlegm. Cold, raw foods and iced drinks can shock the system and worsen palpitations. Instead, favor warm, cooked meals like soups and congees that are easy to digest and nourish the Heart.

research.title: Acupuncture for cardiac arrhythmia: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This systematic review evaluated the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for various cardiac arrhythmias, including premature beats. It found that acupuncture may reduce the frequency of premature contractions and improve symptoms, but the overall quality of evidence was low due to small sample sizes and risk of bias in included studies.
research.periodical: Liu Y, et al. Acupuncture for cardiac arrhythmia: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. J Integr Med. 2018;16(3):153-160.

research.title: Effect of acupuncture at Neiguan (PC6) on premature atrial contractions: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this RCT, 60 patients with symptomatic premature atrial contractions were randomized to receive either real acupuncture at Neiguan (PC6) and adjunct points or sham acupuncture. The real acupuncture group experienced a significantly greater reduction in PAC count on 24-hour Holter monitoring and reported improved palpitation-related quality of life.
research.periodical: Zhang W, et al. Effect of acupuncture at Neiguan (PC6) on premature atrial contractions: a randomized controlled trial. Chin J Integr Med. 2017;23(8):579-584.
